Economic policy to economic statecraft Economic statecraft goes a step further by employing economic tools to achieve foreign policy or national security objectives, such as compelling a country to stop hostilities with a third party or to liberalise its markets. A growing number of nations are becoming increasingly sceptical of free trade and multilateral institutions, which are believed to have led to large and concentrated global trade imbalances. The lack of updated global norms to govern competition, investment, and subsidies across different development models, which led to the build-up of imbalances and strategic distrust, is fostering a more fragmented and polarised global order, accompanied by a weakening, both institutional and financial, of traditional standard setting international bodies. Consequently, geopolitical tensions have intensified

Regarding the industry, a concern is often raised about its declining share in GVA. The compression in manufacturing’s GVA share stems from relative price effects rather than reflecting a decline in manufacturing activities (See section ‘GDP Deflators: Manufacturing’s Reversal in Terms of Trade’ in Chapter V) and higher intermediate consumption, which reduces net value added relative to sectors with greater pricing power, particularly services. In real (constant) price terms, manufacturing’s share has remained steady at around 17-18 per cent (Chart I.16). Manufacturing’s gross value of output (GVO) has remained broadly stable at around 38 per cent, comparable to services, indicating that output has been sustained. Moreover, in FY26, the industrial sector is expected to gain momentum, growing at 6.2 per cent, up from 5.9 per cent in FY25.

Total Factor Productivity (TFP) in India’s Potential Growth What is TFP? The Survey models output with a Cobb–Douglas production function: Y = A · K · L • Y: Output (GDP) • K: Capital stock (machines, infrastructure, etc.) • L: Labour input (workers, hours, quality-adjusted) • A: Total Factor Productivity (TFP) – how efficiently K and L are used Calibrated Trends (Illustrative) Pre-pandemic averages (FY13–FY20): • Capital stock growth ≈ 7.6% per year • Labour input growth ≈ 2.3% per year • Trend TFP growth ≈ 1.9% per year (residual) The Survey assumes that, after COVID disruptions and with reforms, trend TFP growth gradually returns to ~1.9% in FY26– 30, with capital and labour growth close to pre-COVID averages. Why TFP Matters for 7% Potential Growth TFP embodies the impact of: • Digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, GSTN) • Better logistics & physical infrastructure • Regulatory simplification & insolvency reforms • Skilling, formalisation & better allocative efficiency With capital stock growth, labour input growth and trend TFP all strengthened by reforms, the Survey argues that India’s medium-term potential growth has shifted up to around 7%.

From Hyper-Globalisation to Geostrategic Globalisation • Countries remain interconnected but more selective in trade partners • Supply chains evaluated for resilience & strategic autonomy, not just cost • Rise of minilateral platforms: Quad, IPEF • New connectivity corridors: India–Middle East–Europe

# Page 23^page=23
External Sector: Global Trade dynamics

# Page 24^page=24
India's Integration with Global Trade • Share in global merchandise exports: 1% (2005) → 1.8% (2024) • Share in global commercial services: 2% → 4.3% • Strong non-petroleum merchandise & high-value manufacturing exports Diversification of Partners & Products • Trade partner diversity: 3rd in Global South (after China, UAE); score 3.2 • Merchandise product diversity: 4th in Global South; indicator 0.88 • Resilient under tariff uncertainty; scope for more product sophistication

Agricultural Exports – Untapped Potential • FY20–FY25: USD 34.5 bn → USD 51.1 bn (CAGR 8.2%) • India: 2nd largest producer; global export share only 2.2% • Target: USD 100 bn in agri + marine + food exports • Policy issue: Frequent export bans for inflation management disrupt supply chains

# Page 28^page=28
PLI Sectors – Export & Import Growth • PLI scheme: 14 sectors; exports AAGR ~10.6%, imports ~12.6% (FY21–25) • High-growth sectors: IT hardware (~77%), ACC batteries (~45%), electronics (~39%) • Telecom success: exports +1.5%, imports –18.5% (import substitution) Economic Complexity & Export Upgrading • Economic Complexity Index: rank 44/145 (improved from 57, flat since 2019) • Export basket still mid-/low-complexity dominated • Complexity Outlook Index: rank 2nd globally (high future potential) • Need shift to high-complexity: advanced machinery, electronics, chemicals Economic complexity is a measure of the knowledge in a society as expressed in the products it makes. The economic complexity of a country is calculated based on the diversity of exports a country produces and their ubiquity, or the number of countries able to produce them (and those countries’ economic complexity). Countries that are able to sustain a diverse range of productive know-how, including sophisticated, unique know-how, are found to be able to produce a wide diversity of goods, including complex products that few other countries can make.

# Page 29^page=29
FTAs & Export Support • New FTAs: India–UK CETA, India–Oman CEPA signed • India–Oman: 99.38% duty-free access for exports, enhanced services mobility • Export Promotion Mission: unified digital framework for export support • RBI trade relief: credit tenor extension, moratorium, realisation period 9→15 months Pharma Sector – TRIPS Transformation • Shock: Move from process to product patents (1995) • Response: Internal capability building, market diversification, CRAMS model • Outcome: Pharma exports USD 1.9 bn (FY01) → USD 30.5 bn (FY25) • Lesson: Turn external shocks into opportunities via capability, diversification, partnerships

Current Account Development • Structure: Merchandise deficit offset by services & remittance surpluses • H1 FY26: CAD USD 15 bn (0.8% of GDP) vs USD 25.3 bn (1.3%) in H1 FY25 • India's CAD modest & sustainable compared to peers

Global FDI Context • CY24: Global FDI down 11% (2nd year of contraction) • Falls in Europe (–58%), China (–29%); developing economies stable • H1 2025: Further 3% decline; M&A down 23%, greenfield numbers down 17% • But greenfield values +7% (AI, semiconductor, data centres)

# Page 36^page=36
FDI into India – Resilience • FY25: Gross FDI USD 81 bn (+13% YoY); equity FDI USD 51 bn • Apr–Nov 2025: USD 64.7 bn vs USD 55.8 bn previous year • 4th globally in greenfield projects; top for digital greenfield (USD 114 bn, 2020–24) • Returns attractive: avg ~7.3% (2014–23), risk-adjusted return high

# Page 37^page=37
FDI Challenge & Policy Direction • Global competition intense; peers (Vietnam, Malaysia) using aggressive strategies • India strengths: stability, macro fundamentals, growth, market size • Gaps: Below potential, especially infrastructure • Need: High-level coordinated structure, targeted sectoral support, policy predictability

# Page 38^page=38
Outward FDI (ODI) • FY25: USD 23.6 bn (vs 14.4 bn FY24); Apr–Aug FY26: USD 10.2 bn • Reflects internationalisation of Indian firms, tech & market access • Evidence: ODI complements domestic investment, raises exports & R&D • Top destinations: Singapore, US, UAE, Mauritius, Netherlands, UK

# Page 39^page=39
Foreign Portfolio Investment • FPI volatile, tied to global financial cycles (GFC, taper tantrum, COVID, tightening) • FY26 (Apr–Dec): 6 months outflows, 3 months inflows; modest net balance • Driven by US yields, global risk sentiment, not domestic fundamentals • VRR/FAR routes stabilize some debt flows

# Page 40^page=40
Foreign Exchange Reserves • 16 Jan 2026: USD 701.4 bn (vs USD 668.3 bn end-March 2025) • Import cover: ~11 months; covers ~94% of external debt • Gold component rising sharply: USD 78.2 bn → USD 117.5 bn • Adequate liquidity buffer amid volatile capital flows

# Page 41^page=41
Exchange Rate Dynamics • Apr 2025–Jan 2026: INR depreciated ~5.4% vs USD • Drivers: Capital outflows, tariff uncertainty, import pressures, hedging demand • Growth-led import demand (capital goods, intermediates, energy, gold) • Weaker INR beneficial for merchandise trade (elasticity –1.45)

# Page 42^page=42


# Page 43^page=43
Exchange Rate – Long-Term Anchors • Medium-term: Anchored in savings-investment balance & current account • Durable strength requires sustained manufacturing export growth • East Asia lesson: Manufacturing exports + disciplined policy → currency credibility • Services alone insufficient for scale & resilience
